newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians confined to their homes during siege.
newsitem.headline: Albanians confined to their homes during siege.

text.p: Families in Tirana, ever resourceful in fending off deprivation, dug even deeper this week to cope with daily problems during two days of gun rule which confined them to their homes.

"We scraped together money from friends, enough to go out and buy a sack of flour to make bread," said Qefsere in the two-room flat where she lives with four of her six children. "We got someone to bring it around. I didn't even go into the courtyard. Who knows where those stray bullets could land."
The 50-kg (110 lb) sack took up most of a pantry also used to store crockery and linen. In the adjoining kitchen, family meals were prepared on a rudimentary hotplate with two heating elements.

"We're all right really. Between bread and pasta we have enough to keep us going for two weeks," she said. "And a good thing too. We went out for the first time today but the queues were huge, especially for bread. I gave up and came home."

Three of Qesfere's four sons were unemployed. One had just landed a job as a bodyguard at one of Tirana's myriad cafes, built largely on early proceeds from Albania's high-risk pyramid investment schemes, five of which have collapsed.

The family's total monthly income, including her wages from a cleaning job at the Institute of Languages, stood at about the equivalent of $40. There was never a question of investing in the hugely popular pyramids.
"How could we? There wasn't a single lek to put away," she said. "It's just as well."
In the next stairwell, Vasilika, a pensioner, said the hardest part of two days of confinement was soothing her three-year-old grandson during blasts of rapid-fire shooting.
"He would not be consoled at first. We kept telling him it was far away," she said. "He got used to it, like we all did. But there was never any question of going out."

Vasilika spent most of the two days watching television programmes interspersed with appeals for calm and pledges by the all-party government appointed last week after President Sali Berisha abandoned his refusal to work with the opposition.

"Sometimes it was hard to believe those ministers on the television were real," she said. "We'd switch over to the Italian or German channels. They're more realistic. But you still have to hope that this new government will do something."
Vasilika's son lost his job in a bakery when it cut staff in 1990, the same year in which Communist rule ended, and has been unemployed ever since.
Though less reluctant to go out during the shooting, he was now free to spend more on the street meeting his friends, none of whom could afford to sit in a cafe.

In the front room of Qesfere's flat, neat with a spotless tablecloth, daughters Anila, 13, and Mereme, 14, were wishing they were back at school, shut since emergency rule was introduced in Albania two weeks ago to curb the growing unrest.

An uncluttered bedroom was dotted with pictures of British pop stars The Spice Girls and a small cross, although like 70 percent of Albania's 3.4 million people, the family was at least nominally Moslem.
Schoolbooks were tidied away in a small drawer from which Mereme produced her most prized possessions -- sketches she had made of fashion models.

"I'm taking a correspondence course in art," she said in slightly accented English. "We all feel better now that the shooting has stopped, but there's still not a lot to do. We'll go out and perhaps play ball with some friends."
But unlike hard-pressed consumers in some east European countries, most Albanians would never consider a return to the harsh brand of communism practised by Stalinist Enver Hoxha for 45 years.

"I can't forget that we used to have to queue at two in the morning back then just to get milk," Qesfere said. "But when I look at how life is elsewhere on television I wonder whether we'll every have anything like that. Somehow I doubt it."
